openingProblem.problem: In October 1962 the United States and the Soviet Union came closer to nuclear war than at any other time. Thirteen days later the crisis was over. How did it start, and how did both sides step back?

chunks.title: Revolution and confrontation, 1959–1961
chunks.body:
Until 1959 Cuba was closely tied to the United States. That year a left-wing revolution overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista, and **Fidel Castro** became Premier. Castro's government quickly broke Cuba's links with the US: it expropriated American-owned businesses and property and developed close ties with the Soviet Union. Given Cuba's closeness to the United States, this caused grave concern in Washington, and Cuba became, in the Office of the Historian's words, "a new and significant factor in the Cold War".

The US tried to remove Castro. In March 1960 President Eisenhower ordered the CIA to plan an invasion. The CIA trained and funded a force of Cuban exiles, Brigade 2506. After his election in November 1960, John F. Kennedy learned of the plan, concluded that Castro was a Soviet client threatening all of Latin America, and allowed the plan to go ahead. On 17 April 1961 the brigade landed at the **Bay of Pigs**. It was defeated within two days by Cuban forces under Castro's personal command.

The invasion backfired. It strengthened Castro's position, and he now openly proclaimed his intention to build socialism and to seek closer ties with the Soviet Union. For Kennedy it was a serious foreign policy failure and embarrassment.

The failure did not end American efforts. After a review led by General Maxwell Taylor and the President's brother, Attorney General Robert Kennedy, the administration decided in November 1961 on a new covert programme, **Operation Mongoose**. It combined propaganda, sabotage, arms for opposition groups and plans to assassinate Cuban leaders, including Castro, all building towards preparations for a military intervention in October 1962.

This mattered because American hostility convinced Castro and Khrushchev that Cuba needed protection, which meant that US attempts to remove Castro helped create the conditions for the missile crisis.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Castro's early break with the US was over economics as much as ideology.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Kennedy inherited the plan from Eisenhower.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The planned intervention never took place.

chunks.title: Why missiles in Cuba? 1961–1962
chunks.body:
In July 1962 Khrushchev reached a secret agreement with Castro to place Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba. Construction of the sites began in late summer. Why did the Soviet leader take such a risk?

**Defending Cuba.** The Office of the Historian states the official purpose plainly: to deter any future American invasion. After the Bay of Pigs and with Operation Mongoose under way, Cuba had good reason to fear one.

**The nuclear balance.** Kennedy had campaigned in 1960 on the claim of a "missile gap" in the Soviets' favour. But soon after taking office his administration found that the balance of nuclear power still favoured the United States. Missiles in Cuba, close to American cities, would partly redress that balance.

**Bargaining over Europe.** The Office of the Historian also describes the deployment as atomic diplomacy, an attempt "to try to force U.S. concessions on Europe". In Washington, Kennedy and his advisers were convinced that Berlin was the real target. On 19 October Kennedy told his advisers: "Our problem is not merely Cuba but it is also Berlin." Judt argues that they had taken Soviet bluster too seriously: Khrushchev was "entirely rational about Berlin" and had no intention of risking nuclear war for Germany.

**Khrushchev's outlook.** Judt adds a further reason: Khrushchev still believed in the international class struggle, and his "romanticized projection of Soviet revolutionary memories onto Latin American uprisings" led him into the missteps that produced the crisis.

Whatever the motive, the US had warned clearly. On 4 September 1962 Kennedy publicly warned against introducing offensive weapons into Cuba. Throughout the summer US intelligence had reported growing Soviet arms shipments. On 14 October an American U-2 spy plane photographed sites for medium- and intermediate-range ballistic missiles under construction. The photographs reached the White House the next day, and the crisis began.

This mattered because the deployment combined several aims, which meant that each side could misread the other: Washington saw a threat to Berlin, while Moscow saw a defence of Cuba and a correction of the nuclear balance.

chunks.title: Thirteen days, October 1962
chunks.body:
Kennedy gathered his closest advisers to decide what to do. Some, including all the Joint Chiefs of Staff, wanted an air strike to destroy the missiles followed by an invasion of Cuba; others favoured stern warnings. Kennedy chose a middle course. On **22 October** he ordered a naval **"quarantine"** of Cuba. The word was chosen carefully: a blockade implied a state of war, whereas a quarantine did not, and it won the support of the Organization of American States. The same evening Kennedy wrote to Khrushchev demanding that the missile bases be dismantled, and told the American people on television that any missile launched from Cuba would be treated "as an attack by the Soviet Union on the United States, requiring a full retaliatory response". US forces went to DEFCON 3.

On 24 October Khrushchev denounced the "blockade" as an "act of aggression" and said Soviet ships would proceed. Yet on 24 and 25 October some ships turned back from the quarantine line, and those that were stopped carried no offensive weapons. The missile sites, however, were nearing readiness, and US forces moved to **DEFCON 2**: war involving the Strategic Air Command was imminent. On 26 October Kennedy told his advisers that only an attack seemed likely to remove the missiles, but he gave diplomacy more time.

That day a way out appeared. A Soviet agent told the ABC journalist John Scali that the Soviets might remove the missiles if the US promised not to invade Cuba. That evening Khrushchev sent Kennedy a long, emotional message: "let us not only relax the forces pulling on the ends of the rope, let us take measures to untie that knot." He wrote that if war broke out, "it would not be in our power to stop it, for such is the logic of war."

**27 October** was the most dangerous day. Khrushchev sent a second message demanding the removal of American Jupiter missiles from Turkey, and a U-2 was shot down over Cuba. Kennedy and his advisers prepared for an attack within days. They decided to ignore the second message and answer the first: the Soviets would remove their missiles under UN supervision, and the US would guarantee not to attack Cuba. Robert Kennedy then met the Soviet ambassador, Anatoly Dobrynin, in secret and told him that the US would soon remove the Jupiters from Turkey anyway, but that this could not be part of any public deal. On the morning of **28 October** Khrushchev announced that the missiles would be dismantled.

This mattered because the crisis was resolved by private communication between the two leaders, which meant that the decisive deal included a secret concession that neither side made public.

chunks.title: Who won? Consequences of the crisis
chunks.body:
On the surface, the United States won. The Soviet missiles were removed, the quarantine ended on 20 November 1962 once the Soviets agreed to take away their IL-28 bombers as well, and the crisis strengthened Kennedy's image at home and abroad. It may also have helped repair the damage the Bay of Pigs had done to his reputation.

But the outcome was more balanced than it looked. Khrushchev obtained a public American guarantee not to invade Cuba, which had been the stated purpose of the missiles, and the Jupiter missiles were quietly removed from Turkey in April 1963. Castro remained in power; Operation Mongoose's planned intervention never took place. Yet because the Turkish part of the deal was secret, the world saw a Soviet retreat. Judt notes that Khrushchev's missteps in Cuba helped bring about his own downfall.

The most important consequences were for the relationship between the superpowers. During the crisis Kennedy and Khrushchev had struggled to understand each other's real intentions while the world stood on the brink of nuclear war. To avoid that happening again, a direct telephone link, the **Hotline**, was set up between the White House and the Kremlin on 20 June 1963. Having come so close to nuclear conflict, both sides began to reconsider the arms race. A month later, talks in Moscow produced the **Limited Test Ban Treaty**, in force from 10 October 1963. Judt argues that its unspoken purpose was to keep nuclear weapons away from China and West Germany.

The crisis also showed how the Cold War had changed. Judt argues that Washington felt it had to "stand firm" over Berlin and Cuba to reassure allies who feared the US might abandon them; and that Kennedy's fixation on Berlin had magnified the stakes of the crisis. At the same time, Khrushchev's genuine aversion to war, shown in his message of 26 October, was a reason the crisis ended peacefully.

This mattered because both leaders had looked into the abyss and stepped back, which meant that the crisis led to the first steps towards arms control and, in time, détente.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was the Bay of Pigs invasion the main reason for the Cuban Missile Crisis between 1961 and 1962?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The Bay of Pigs, weighed first
decodeKey.judgement: Whether the invasion outweighed Soviet strategic aims

modelPlan.thesis: The Bay of Pigs began a sustained US threat to Cuba, continued by Operation Mongoose, which gave Khrushchev his stated reason for the missiles; but Soviet strategic aims, especially narrowing the US nuclear lead, explain why he chose nuclear missiles.

arguments.claim: The Bay of Pigs and its aftermath (named factor first).
Operation Mongoose and the continuing threat.
The nuclear balance.
Khrushchev's outlook.

modelPlan.counter: Washington believed Berlin, not Cuba, was the real Soviet target.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Why nuclear missiles rather than conventional defence? Because they also served Soviet strategic aims.

segments.text: The Bay of Pigs was an important cause of the crisis, but not the main one.
The failed invasion of 17 April 1961 strengthened Castro and pushed him towards Moscow, and Operation Mongoose kept the threat alive.
This meant that Khrushchev could justify the missiles as a defence of Cuba, as the secret agreement of July 1962 stated.

However, nuclear missiles were far more than Cuba needed for defence; the US held the nuclear lead, and the deployment was also, in the Office of the Historian's words, an attempt 'to force U.S. concessions on Europe'.
The Bay of Pigs was therefore the occasion of the crisis, while Soviet strategic aims were its main cause.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “Khrushchev was the loser of the Cuban Missile Crisis.” Discuss with reference to the period 1961 to 1962.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: By what criterion: appearance, substance, or his career?

modelPlan.thesis: Khrushchev lost the propaganda battle and damaged his career, but in substance he achieved Cuba's security and the removal of the Jupiters, so the claim holds for appearance rather than outcome.

arguments.claim: For: the public retreat of 28 October.
For: damage to his career.
Against: the no-invasion pledge.
Against: the secret removal of the Jupiters.

modelPlan.counter: Kennedy's image was strengthened, which suggests the world judged the US the winner.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: By appearance, he lost; by substance, he gained most of what the missiles were meant to achieve.

segments.text: Khrushchev lost in appearance but not in substance.
On 28 October he announced that the missiles would be dismantled, but he had a public US pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret promise to remove the Jupiters from Turkey.
This meant that the stated purpose of the missiles was achieved, while the Turkish concession stayed hidden, so the world saw a Soviet retreat.
However, Judt argues that Khrushchev's missteps in Cuba helped bring about his downfall, so politically he paid a price.
The claim is therefore valid for his reputation and career, but not for the deal itself.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate Kennedy's handling of the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: By what criterion: avoiding war, or winning?

modelPlan.thesis: Kennedy handled the crisis skilfully, rejecting an air strike for a quarantine and answering Khrushchev's more conciliatory message; but the settlement rested on a secret concession over Turkey, so it was a compromise, not a pure victory.

arguments.claim: The quarantine as a middle course.
Firmness: the television warning and DEFCON.
Diplomacy: answering the first message.
Limits: the secret concession; the Bay of Pigs background.

modelPlan.counter: Kennedy's earlier decisions, the Bay of Pigs and Mongoose, helped cause the crisis.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: By the criterion of avoiding war, Kennedy succeeded; by the criterion of an outright win, he compromised.

segments.text: Kennedy handled the crisis skilfully, judged by the aim of removing the missiles without war.
He rejected the Joint Chiefs' call for an air strike, ordered a 'quarantine' on 22 October and, on 27 October, answered Khrushchev's first message rather than the second.
This meant that Khrushchev was offered a way out, so on 28 October he agreed to remove the missiles.
However, the deal depended on a secret promise to remove the Jupiters from Turkey, and Kennedy's own Bay of Pigs and Mongoose had helped cause the crisis.
Kennedy's handling was therefore successful in October 1962, though his wider Cuba policy shared the blame for the crisis.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the causes and consequences of the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The crisis was caused by the Soviet decision to place missiles in Cuba, to protect Castro from a real US threat and to narrow the US nuclear lead; its main consequence was the first steps towards managing the arms race.

arguments.claim: Cause: the US threat to Cuba.
Cause: Soviet strategic aims.
Consequence: a compromise settlement.
Consequence: the Hotline and Test Ban.

modelPlan.counter: Misperception over Berlin made the crisis more dangerous than its causes alone explain.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? The beginning of arms control, which led towards détente.

segments.text: The crisis was caused by Khrushchev's decision to place missiles in Cuba, both to protect Castro and to narrow the US nuclear lead.
After the Bay of Pigs and Operation Mongoose, Khrushchev agreed with Castro in July 1962 to deploy missiles, which a U-2 photographed on 14 October.
This meant that the US faced nuclear missiles close to its cities, so it imposed a quarantine and reached DEFCON 2 before the deal of 28 October.
However, Judt argues that Kennedy's belief that Berlin was the real target magnified the crisis.
Its most significant consequence was therefore the Hotline and the Test Ban, the first steps towards managing the arms race.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the aims of the United States and the Soviet Union in Cuba between 1959 and 1962.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The aims of the two superpowers

modelPlan.thesis: Both superpowers treated Cuba as a test of credibility, but the US sought to remove Castro while the USSR sought to protect him and use Cuba to narrow the nuclear balance; in the end both settled for Castro staying and the missiles leaving.

arguments.claim: Similarity: Cuba as a test of credibility.
Similarity: both used covert methods.
Difference: remove Castro against protect him.
Difference: strategic aims over the nuclear balance.

modelPlan.counter: Both were also thinking of Europe: the US of Berlin, the USSR of concessions there.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? Over Castro: the settlement turned on a pledge not to invade.

segments.text: Both superpowers saw Cuba as a test of their credibility, but their aims were opposite.
The US backed the Bay of Pigs and Operation Mongoose to remove Castro, whereas Khrushchev agreed in July 1962 to place missiles in Cuba to deter an invasion.
This meant that the crisis turned on Castro's survival, so the settlement of 28 October included a US pledge not to invade.
However, both were also thinking of Europe: Washington feared a Soviet move on Berlin, while Moscow hoped for concessions there.
The decisive difference was therefore over Castro, which the settlement resolved in the Soviet Union's favour.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons why the Cuban Missile Crisis did not lead to nuclear war in 1962.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: War was avoided because Kennedy chose a quarantine rather than an air strike, both leaders feared war and kept communicating, and a public pledge combined with a secret concession let Khrushchev retreat.

arguments.claim: Kennedy's middle course.
Both leaders' fear of war.
Back channels and the choice of the first message.
The secret Jupiter concession.

modelPlan.counter: Chance played a part: a U-2 was shot down on 27 October, and war was days away.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which reason mattered most? The secret concession, because it let Khrushchev retreat without public humiliation.

segments.text: The crisis did not lead to nuclear war mainly because both leaders found a way for Khrushchev to retreat.
Kennedy chose a quarantine over an air strike, answered Khrushchev's first message, and Robert Kennedy secretly promised the removal of the Jupiters.
This meant that Khrushchev gained a no-invasion pledge and a hidden concession, so on 28 October he agreed to withdraw.
However, war was close: US forces were at DEFCON 2 and a U-2 was shot down on 27 October, so luck as well as skill mattered.
War was therefore avoided by a combination of restraint, communication and a compromise that neither side made fully public.
